# **ABSTRACT** {#abstract}

This study developed and evaluated a multimodal computer-vision prototype for pickleball serve classification and rule-based practice feedback. The selected original five-fold GRU ensemble operates with a 0.60 confidence gate and separate hip-movement and image-plane paddle measurements. The earlier GRU–kNN5 hybrid remains a comparison. Historical original-GRU stratified cross-validation was 86.7%, while a matched, previously inspected 175-clip diagnostic set yielded 51.4%, compared with 46.9% for the retrained v2 ensemble and 49.7% for the hybrid. On 30 selected clips, the system produced 19 corrective, two positive, eight low-confidence and one partial output, giving 70.0% substantive coaching coverage. Coach C judged 27 clips Bad Form and three Good Form in Session 1. Session 2 returned 27 Valid, one Not valid and two No coaching feedback to assess responses: 90.0% rated Valid across all clips and 96.4% among Valid/Not valid answers. Eight Valid answers concerned notice-only outputs and two corrective outputs were marked no coaching, limiting interpretation of these percentages. The current form's 30 outputs matched frozen reports; historical submission-time presentation was not independently reconstructed. Xiaomi recorded-video processing had a 68.576-second optimized median, with no meaningful total improvement over baseline. This timing does not verify the proposed live two-second target. A post-review live-path phone replay on the same 30 clips increased corrective-feedback availability from 2/30 to 18/30 using GPU acquisition, time-normalized capture and guarded general cues. Eleven outputs bypassed uncertain subtype classification only for rules applicable to all serve types. These new outputs were not expert-rated; three clips produced no completed output and one result appeared 3.126 seconds after file end. The study demonstrates a limited prototype and completed descriptive review, with partially attained objectives; it does not establish independent Coach C subtype accuracy, improved serving performance or coach replacement.

# **CHAPTER 1** {#chapter-1}

# **INTRODUCTION**

	This chapter establishes the foundational context for the study, outlining the rapid global and local growth of pickleball alongside the critical shortage of accessible, certified coaching. It defines the core problem, the absence of an automated tool for serve-specific biomechanical evaluation,and details the study's general and specific objectives. Furthermore, it articulates the significance of the proposed multimodal computer vision system for players, coaches, and future researchers, while clearly defining the scope, hardware constraints, and boundaries of the research.

## **1.1 Rationale of the Study** {#1.1-rationale-of-the-study}

Pickleball is a comparatively young sport that has undergone extraordinary recent growth. The Sports & Fitness Industry Association has identified it as the fastest-growing sport in the United States for five consecutive years, reporting an expansion of the player base from 4.2 million in 2020 to over 24.3 million by 2025 (SFIA, 2026). This pattern is not confined to the United States. In the Philippines, pickleball has similarly been described as one of the country's fastest-growing sports, with industry sources projecting the domestic player base to surpass 200,000 by 2030 (Context.Ph, 2026). Institutional structures have followed: the Philippine Pickleball Federation, a member of both the Philippine Olympic Committee and the Global Pickleball Federation, launched the Philippine Pickleball Participant Registry and implemented an Official National Ranking System in January 2026 (Martin, 2026), signalling a push toward standardized coaching and officiating pathways as the sport scales locally.

As in the United States, however, this rapid growth in participation has outpaced the availability of certified instruction, reinforcing the same accessibility gap within a domestic context. With the Professional Pickleball Registry (PPR) reporting over 10,000 certified coaches as of January 2025 against the massive player base, the ratio is over 2,000 players per coach, creating a severe shortage of accessible, individualized instruction (PPR, 2025). One contributing factor to this accessibility gap is the lack of tools that give players real-time, skill-specific feedback outside of live coaching.

The shortage of human coaching has coincided with rapid technological advances, with the sport increasingly leaning on digital platforms like the Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating (DUPR) and smart apps like PB Vision. While these existing technologies are highly capable of generating high-level match analytics, shot statistics, and skill ratings, technology specifically engineered for prescriptive coaching assistance, such as serve classification and rule-based form feedback, has not yet been developed.

Related computer vision research has begun to address components of this gap in isolation. Recent advancements in Human Pose Estimation (HPE) can now track skeletal keypoints and extract biomechanical data using standard video inputs, offering a non-invasive alternative to physical wearable sensors. However, prior work has only applied pose estimation to individual, controlled pickleball shots like the dink. Evaluating the high-velocity, ballistic motion of a serve introduces additional complexity, requiring the simultaneous tracking of the player's skeletal sequence and bodyweight transfer, the capture of paddle orientation, and, as an extended capability, the spatial mapping of ball placement.  Furthermore, while validated biomechanical serve taxonomies exist for tennis, direct transferability to pickleball is severely limited because the equipment mechanics and serve rules differ substantially between the two sports.

To investigate accessible serve analysis, this study combines pose-based classification with separate movement and paddle measurements. The selected subtype classifier uses the original five-fold GRU ensemble without kNN fusion. The wider multimodal pipeline combines the resulting prediction with available measurements at the decision level, where researcher-authored IF-THEN rules informed by coach commentary select practice cues. This architecture supports inspection of each output and of missing measurements. It does not itself establish improved accuracy or valid coaching; these are separate evaluation questions.

## **1.2 Problem Statement** {#1.2-problem-statement}

Despite the emergence of generalized analytics platforms like DUPR and PB Vision (PB Vision, 2026), and initial pose-estimation research applied to controlled pickleball shots (Edriss et al., 2025), no existing computational system combines multiple modalities for serve-specific evaluation. Furthermore, established racket-sport taxonomies (such as tennis's flat, slice, and topspin) fail to map accurately to pickleball's unique service rules and solid-paddle equipment constraints. By adopting a sport-specific taxonomy, specifically the Drive, Lob, and Topspin serves recognized in pickleball coaching literature, this study addresses the lack of native biomechanical classification. Consequently, players attempting to self-correct their mechanics lack a low-cost, non-expert alternative to live coaching, leaving them without the skill-differentiated feedback needed to correct serve execution errors. 

### **1.2.1 General Objective**  {#1.2.1-general-objective}

This study develops and evaluates a multimodal pickleball serve-analysis prototype using the original five-fold GRU classifier, deterministic hip-movement and image-plane paddle measurements, and coach-informed rules for practice feedback. Ball-placement mapping is an auxiliary capability requiring suitable additional video and is excluded from the current 30-clip evaluation.

### **1.2.2 Specific Objectives:** {#1.2.2-specific-objectives:}

Specifically, this study:

* Examines classification of the recorded Drive, Lob and Topspin categories, while documenting the absence of independent expert subtype labels and the limits of the category reference.
* Organizes recordings, participant membership and form annotations, distinguishing the annotated training inventory, legacy model population and previously exposed evaluation material.
* Uses the original five-fold GRU ensemble for subtype classification and combines its output with available hip and paddle measurements for deterministic feedback. Retains GRU–kNN5 as a separately reported comparison.
* Reports GRU development cross-validation and separate participant-held-out and matched diagnostic comparisons, including hybrid performance. The original 85% stratified-GRU target is retained with its stated scope; it is not redefined as a measured hybrid result.
* Evaluates the contextual validity of displayed feedback through Coach C’s two-session review, reporting valid, invalid, unavailable-coaching and missing-response counts separately. Session 2 is complete; recorded-file Android timing is available, while the live two-second timing boundary remains unverified.

  ## **1.3 Significance of the Study** {#1.3-significance-of-the-study}


  *Players*  
For players, the prototype is intended to provide automatic practice cues from recorded serves. Current cues concern a limited set of hip-movement and paddle-reference observations. It does not directly measure foot loading, diagnose physical paddle-face opening or closing, judge overall form, or establish reliable replacement of an instructor. Its practical value depends on both feedback validity and the proportion of attempts receiving assessable coaching.

  *Coaches*

For coaches, the prototype provides an inspectable implementation of selected coach-informed rules. Coach B’s form commentary informs rule construction, while Coach C reviews the evaluation clips and displayed outputs separately. Session 2 will assess contextual validity; expert approval of every cue cannot be assumed before those responses are collected.


  *Pickleball Organizations and Academies*

For pickleball organizations and academies, the project provides a documented prototype and evaluation procedure for studying automatic practice feedback. Use in instruction or certification would require further validation across players and recording conditions. The current study does not establish a standardized biomechanical assessment or certification instrument.


  


  *Future Researchers*

For future researchers, the study contributes an auditable comparison of GRU, kNN5 fusion and separate development candidates; a pipeline connecting limited video measurements to deterministic feedback; and records of coaching coverage and expert form judgments. Recorded categories are distinguished from independently assigned subtype labels. The experiments expose participant-transfer and confidence-gating limitations, while physical-device latency and Session 2 feedback validity remain open measurements. Data availability is governed by the retained consent and repository arrangements; a complete public release is not assumed.


  Two further practitioner-identified serve variations were deliberately excluded and remain direct extensions for future work. The Sidespin serve is distinguished primarily by lateral spin direction, which a monocular camera cannot measure. The Short-Angled serve is distinguished by tactical placement intent rather than by a mechanically distinct swing profile, so it is not separable from the retained subtypes on pose kinematics or paddle orientation alone. Left-handed support is a direct extension as well; the keypoint-based architecture makes coordinate mirroring feasible in principle, but would require dedicated left-handed recording and coach validation to confirm that mirrored right-handed form baselines transfer correctly. 


  


  ## **1.4 Scope and Limitations** {#1.4-scope-and-limitations}


This study focuses on recorded pickleball serves categorized as Drive, Lob and Topspin. The initial proposal included independent expert subtype labeling and a taxonomy fallback. That labeling question was removed from the actual coach instruments, so the fallback gate was not established as a completed validation step. Classification experiments use their recorded category references; the study cannot claim independent validation of the taxonomy from Coach C’s form judgments.

The study excludes other strokes and does not act as a serve-legality adjudicator. Recordings cover right-handed participants at the stated venues. Coach A supplies professional demonstrations and a subset of explicitly good-form reference recordings; professional status alone is not a form label. Coach B supplies construction-set form judgments and comments. Coach C supplies independent form judgments in Session 1 and reviews model feedback in Session 2. Neither actual instrument collects separate subtype labels, and Session 2 is output-informed rather than blinded to the model’s advice.

The implemented mobile proof of concept uses native Android/Kotlin and TFLite assets, alongside a Python recorded-clip runner used for the Coach C batch. The selected classifier averages the five original GRU folds without kNN weighting. The Android default and the recorded-clip default both select this ensemble; capture-window parity is not assumed. Recorded-file benchmarking is complete on the Xiaomi Note 12 running Android 14; the optimized median was 68.576 seconds across nine measured runs of three clips. The second planned device profile and live capture-end-to-displayed-feedback timing remain unverified. Successful builds do not establish the live latency target.

  As a proof of concept, the primary contribution is demonstrated technical feasibility of the pipeline, subtype classification and rule-based feedback generation from video, rather than a complete end-user product. Accordingly, the interface artefacts in Section 4.5.3 are limited to output-state diagrams documenting how the four core system outputs and the partial-delivery behaviour in FR7 are surfaced to the user. Production-oriented design artefacts such as full navigation flows and use case diagrams remain outside scope, as they suit projects specifying multi-screen interface layouts and detailed actor-system interaction for a deployed application.

The present evaluation uses prepared recordings. Live ingestion, autonomous triggering and automatic capture termination are production requirements rather than demonstrated results of this evaluation. The desktop and Android capture windows differ, so identical preprocessing and end-to-end behavior cannot be assumed. Immediate feedback is a latency objective to be measured after capture, not an established capability of continuous live analysis.


  


  


  *Limitations*

  The findings and operational capabilities of this study are subject to several inherent limitations beyond the researchers' control.

* **Single-Camera Core Architecture:** The evaluated hip and paddle measurements are image-plane proxies from the primary view. They do not establish physical weight distribution, three-dimensional paddle-face orientation or ball spin. Auxiliary landing is disabled for all 30 clips; synchronized second-camera mobile operation is not validated here.
* **Single-Expert Annotation Constraint:** Coach B supplies construction-set form judgments and Coach C supplies evaluation judgments on different clips. This does not support inter-rater reliability. Independent subtype labels were omitted, and recorded category labels must retain their actual provenance. Reference measurements from explicitly good-form Coach A clips do not establish a consensus biomechanical standard.
* **Annotation and Population Constraints:** The supplied recording inventory reports 812 clips, with a 210-clip construction annotation allocation and 30 evaluation clips. Legacy classifiers use a distinct 438-sample population, and 175 beginner clips have diagnostic exposure. These overlapping scopes cannot be summed or described as though every recording outside the annotation allocation was computationally unused. Only three participants contribute to the principal training inventory.
* **Environmental and Extraction Vulnerabilities:** Because recordings are captured exclusively under artificial court lighting regardless of time of day, the dataset introduces known vulnerabilities to motion blur and reduced contrast, which may degrade paddle angle estimations when OpenCV's minAreaRect processes high-velocity swing contours. These vulnerabilities apply equally to the auxiliary ball detection module when a secondary camera is in use.   
* **Hardware-Specific Latency Constraints:** Recorded-file measurements are available for one Xiaomi Note 12. Live capture-to-display behavior and the second planned device profile remain unverified; these measurements do not establish minimum operating specifications.
* **Handedness:** All participants are right-handed, and horizontal-flip augmentation is deliberately excluded (Section 4.3.2). The trained classifier is therefore not expected to generalize to left-handed players, and left-handed support would require additional collection.   
* **Unrepresented Movement and Body Configurations:** The study has not validated performance for participants using prostheses or with limb differences, or for other body configurations and movement conditions absent from its sample. Tracking and coaching reliability for those populations cannot be inferred from the current data.

# **CHAPTER 2** {#chapter-2}

# **REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE** {#review-of-related-literature}

This chapter synthesizes existing research and technological advancements pertinent to the study, establishing the academic and practical foundation for the proposed system. It explores the necessity of a pickleball-native serve taxonomy and reviews the current landscape of human pose estimation (HPE) and action recognition in racket sports. By analyzing prior automated coaching applications, monocular spatial mapping techniques, and the complexities of late-stage signal fusion, this review highlights the critical gaps in the current literature that this study addresses. 

***Pickleball Serve Taxonomy and Biomechanical Classification Basis*** 

	Biomechanics serves as a foundation for sports analysis, quantifying sport-specific movement. In racket sports, serves are an essential skill to master for success, as their execution may be influenced by various factors such as their type, direction, and stance style (Lambrich & Muehlbauer, 2023). At a regulatory level, USA Pickleball formally defines two legal methods for initiating a serve: the volley serve and the drop serve (USA Pickleball, 2026). However, these are strictly rule-based categories governing serve initiation; they do not describe the mechanical execution or biomechanical profile of the stroke itself, leaving a gap between what the rulebook defines and what a coaching system must classify.

Establishing a biomechanical taxonomy native to pickleball requires accounting for the sport's fundamental equipment constraints. Unlike strung tennis rackets that utilize string-bed shear to impart spin, pickleball paddles are solid and strictly regulated by the USA Pickleball Equipment Standards Manual (2025b) regarding surface roughness and the Paddle/Ball Coefficient of Restitution (PBCoR) to limit artificial spin generation. Consequently, pickleball players must rely entirely on distinct kinematic swing paths and paddle face orientations to differentiate their serves, rendering tennis-derived taxonomies like Lambrich & Muehlbauer's (2023) flat, slice, and topspin framework mechanically and legally problematic in a pickleball context, particularly given that USA Pickleball Rule 7.C mandates a continuous upward arc and prohibits chopping mechanics (USA Pickleball, 2026). This study therefore grounds its taxonomy in pickleball-native coaching literature. Nicole Havlicek, a former nationally ranked Division 1 tennis player, IPTPA-certified pickleball coach, and 5.0 DUPR rated competitive player, identifies the Drive, Lob, and Topspin serves as mechanically distinct stroke variations, differentiated by swing plane steepness and paddle face angle at contact (PrimeTime Pickleball, 2023). While Cobar et al. (2025) demonstrated that pickleball stroke kinematics are broadly related to other racket-type sports from a side-view camera, and while this practitioner-derived taxonomy has not yet been validated in peer-reviewed biomechanics literature, it aligns with the sport's mechanical realities more accurately than any imported framework. For the present study, these terms define recorded categories rather than independently validated biomechanical classes. The initially proposed coach-label distinguishability gate and legal-category fallback were not completed under the revised instrument, which collects form judgments and comments without independent subtype labels.

Biomechanical research in racket sports has consistently demonstrated that the serve is not an upper-body action alone. Roetert et al. (2009) established that approximately 51% of kinetic energy during the tennis serve originates from the trunk and legs, with the shoulder contributing only 13%, confirming the lower body as the dominant mechanical contributor to serve power. Kwon (2026) further situates this within a proximal-to-distal kinetic chain framework, where ground reaction forces and lower-limb extension initiate the sequence and disruptions to that sequence reduce serve velocity while increasing mechanical load on the upper extremity. However, existing pose-based automated coaching systems have focused exclusively on upper-body keypoints and swing mechanics, leaving lower-body weight transfer entirely unmeasured and untreated as a classifiable biomechanical signal in any automated pipeline for racket or paddle sports, a motivation for the present hip-movement proxy. This proxy does not directly measure kinetic energy, ground reaction force or weight distribution, and findings from tennis are not treated as its validation.  

***Sports Video Action Recognition and Pickleball's Absence***

Sports analysis is a broad, well-researched field used to quantify performance, automate notational analysis, and support coaching decisions. As such, it heavily relies on video analysis to extract spatiotemporal insights such as players’ kinematics and biomechanics in order to perform tasks such as action recognition and trajectory tracking. Wu et al. (2022) conducted a comprehensive survey covering multiple datasets across 10+ sports with decades of research, finding that the study of video sport analytics is a mature and well-researched field that has been used to provide better analysis for sports coaching. A systematic review conducted by Aulton et al. (2025) examines the applications of deep learning-based Human Pose Estimation (HPE) across multiple sports, including racket-type sports, such as badminton, tennis, and even paddleball; however, pickleball was never mentioned in this review. A recent study conducted by Edriss et al. (2025) utilized video analysis for pickleball kinematic data inference. However, they were limited to dink shots only, without extending the analysis to other shot types such as the serve. Their research also only produces raw kinematic numbers for a coach to interpret, rather than an automated classification or feedback system. Consequently, no study has extended biomechanical video classification beyond dink shots to address pickleball serve types specifically. 

***Pose Estimation as the Primary Signal for Sports Movement Analysis***

	Human Pose Estimation (HPE) models are used in sports to analyze the biomechanics of players in a non-invasive way, replacing physical sensors and extracting data through standard video inputs. MediaPipe is a framework that provides a real-time processing pipeline that manages graph-based calculators, streaming, and GPU support, making mobile device HPE model deployment such as BlazePose possible (Lugaresi et al., 2019). BlazePose is a specific CNN architecture that extracts 33 keypoints in real-time on mobile devices with accuracy validated on a wide variety of poses in the wild and yoga/fitness datasets (Bazarevsky et al., 2020). While validated on general movement, its accuracy on sport-specific, high-velocity motion is what Edriss et al. began to test. Edriss et al. (2025) successfully applied MediaPipe to racket sports, specifically extracting lower-body kinematics and wrist motion during pickleball dink shots. However, the dink is a soft, controlled shot, and their study produced raw kinematic output only; therefore, accuracy on a fast, ballistic motion like a serve, and the translation of that raw output into classification, remains untested. 

***Stroke Classification from Pose in Racket Sports***

	Kulkarni and Shenoy (2021), Mone et al. (2025), and Chang (2026) collectively support that temporal modeling of pose keypoint sequences leads to high-accuracy and fine-grained stroke classification in racket sports, outperforming general-purpose skeleton-action baselines such as ST-GCN (Yan et al., 2018). Kulkarni and Shenoy (2021) achieve 99.37% accuracy using upper-body pose keypoints alone from a single front-view camera, while Chang (2026) finds that fusing pose with ball trajectory data outperforms pose alone using a single broadcast camera. While both rely on a single camera, the key difference is input composition (pose alone vs pose plus trajectory). This makes Kulkarni and Shenoy's setup closer to this study's core single-camera pipeline, while Chang's findings establish that supplementing pose with ball-related spatial data improves classification, a direction this study acknowledges but does not pursue within the core pipeline given the monocular depth constraints established by Grad et al. (2026). None of these architectures have been applied to pickleball serve-type classification from a side-view single camera, a gap this study addresses.

***Ball Tracking and Court Spatial Mapping***

	Ning et al. (2023) and Alemán-Flores et al. (2014) establish that the two components landing-spot detection requires, ball localization and court- coordinate mapping, are technically tractable from standard video input.  Alemán-Flores et al. (2014) achieve accurate court geometry calibration using line-based homography without requiring 3D flight modeling, while Ning et al. (2023) demonstrate real-time landing point detection for a small, fast-moving ball in a paddle sport using spatial domain information and inter-frame analysis on a low-cost monocular camera. However, Grad et al. (2026) show that monocular ambiguity limits full 3D trajectory reconstruction, where simpler models outperform spin-decomposition ones, suggesting trajectory reconstruction is the harder problem while court-coordinate calibration and landing point detection remain tractable from one camera. Still, no existing system integrates ball landing detection with court-coordinate calibration into a pose-based paddle-sport coaching pipeline, whether under monocular or multi-camera conditions, leaving serve legality confirmation and placement evaluation unaddressed in pickleball analytics. This study addresses that gap by implementing ball placement as an optional auxiliary module, activated when a secondary camera is available, rather than imposing it as a core single-camera dependency.

***Why Multi-Signal Fusion Is Necessary***

	Yang & Gulbahar (2025) and Li et al. (2023) both demonstrate that fusing heterogeneous signal types consistently outperforms any single signal alone through ablation. Yang & Gulbahar found fused audio-video inputs reached 96.55% accuracy against 37.93% for audio alone and 53.45% for video alone, while Li et al. found key point augmentation (KPA) with hardware sensor data (HSD) outperformed either modality in isolation. However, the two studies disagree on where the fusion should happen. Yang & Gulbahar found late fusion, where each modality is encoded independently and combined only at the decision stage, outperformed early and hybrid fusion due to the imbalanced informativeness in their modalities, with video overpowering audio. Li et al.'s best result however came from a feature-level fusion due to the two streams (KPA & HSD) being closer in dimensionality, removing the risk of one signal overpowering the other. This study’s signals differ sharply in dimensionality with pose’s full keypoint sequence having more dimensions than the paddle’s near-scalar angle, a structure closer to Yang & Gulbahar’s imbalance case than to Li et al.’s. When the auxiliary ball placement module is active under a dual-camera setup, a third signal, the landing point's coordinate pair, is introduced, compounding that imbalance further and reinforcing the case for late fusion as the appropriate integration strategy. Yet no existing study has tested signal fusion timing for three modalities this heterogeneous, nor applied it to stroke or serve classification in any racket or paddle sport. 

***Coaching Applications***

	Augmented coaching tools are a recognized and distinct application of deep learning-based human pose estimation (DL-HPE), with recent systematic evidence confirming that individual, self-paced, skill-based sports like table tennis and badminton are the most common domains for these systems, especially when validated on real participants over datasets alone (Aulton et al., 2025). The importance on timing and technique-specific feedback also appears in Baily and Lai (2022), showing ball-contact timing is the primary factor distinguishing professional, semi-professional, and amateur tennis players, rather than overall swing shape, suggesting that fine-grained temporal features are more diagnostic of skill than overall movement patterns. Wang et al. (2019) turned this logic into a full coaching pipeline, pairing a spatial-temporal pose estimation model with an SVM classifier to detect "bad poses" in freestyle skiing and returning corrective video feedback to the athlete, a structure broadly consistent with a classify-then-correct approach to skill coaching. However, these systems differ in important ways. Wang et al.'s classifier judged pose quality solely using joint-angle thresholds, while Baily and Lai's approach was retrospective, classifying skill level after the fact rather than supporting feedback during training. Aulton et al. (2025) warns that coaching tools offering only prescriptive, error-correcting feedback risk dependency on the technology rather than developing intrinsic self-correction, a critique that applies to systems structured similarly to Wang et al.'s. Despite this, no reviewed study integrates form classification, paddle orientation, and ball-landing location into a single coaching feedback loop for any racket or paddle sport. Furthermore, no study has applied pose-based coaching specifically for pickleball serve mechanics. These gaps motivate the present study's design of a coaching system that links biomechanical serve classification to spatial serve outcomes, providing context-aware and individualized feedback.

# **CHAPTER 3** {#chapter-3}

# **TECHNICAL BACKGROUND** {#technical-background}

	This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the theoretical concepts and computational frameworks that drive the developed multimodal evaluation system. It defines core computer vision mechanisms, including Human Pose Estimation, planar homography, object detection, and temporal sequence modeling via Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs). Additionally, it examines the specific technologies selected for implementation, such as MediaPipe, YOLOv26s, and TensorFlow Lite, while discussing the inherent architectural challenges of edge-device processing, depth ambiguity, and heterogeneous signal fusion. 

## **3.1 Introduction to the Domain** {#3.1-introduction-to-the-domain}

Driven by recent advancements in artificial intelligence, Computer Vision (CV) and video analytics are now applied broadly across a diverse range of complex applications, such as in medical imaging and in autonomous vehicles. One notable example of this rapid integration is in the field of sports analytics (Rossi et al., 2025). In modern sports, these technologies are utilized to accurately quantify both individual and team performance data, such as player velocity, spatial positioning, and tactical execution. By automating video analysis, a process that required countless hours of manual labor, teams can now efficiently generate actionable insights to maximize potential and gain a competitive advantage (Olthof & Davis, 2025). Extracting meaningful data from this complex footage relies on a combination of several distinct computer vision techniques working in concert. Ultimately, this synthesized approach enables analysts to process massive volumes of video into reliable, high-quality intelligence.

## **3.2 Core Concepts & Definitions** {#3.2-core-concepts-&-definitions}

**Human Pose Estimation (HPE)**

Human Pose Estimation (HPE) is a branch of computer vision focused on detecting and tracking keypoints of the human body, which typically include the major joints (e.g., shoulders, knees) and extremities (Zheng et al., 2023). HPE employs various computational frameworks, most commonly deep learning models, to identify the two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) coordinates of anatomical landmarks or keypoints. Using these coordinates of detected keypoints, the system forms a skeletal representation that encodes body configuration over time.

**Classification**

Classification is a supervised machine learning task where a model learns to assign a discrete label from a predefined set of categories to a given input (Sarker, 2021). In supervised classification, a model is trained on labeled examples (input-output pairs) so that it can generalize the learned mapping to unseen inputs at inference time. The model maps inputs to one of the predefined categories based on the patterns learned during training.

**Human Action Recognition (HAR)** 

Human Action Recognition is a computer vision task that interprets human actions by detecting static and dynamic features across video frames (Wang & Yan, 2023). HAR systems typically take either RGB video or skeletal input; with skeletal input, the system processes the geometric relationships and changes of 2D or 3D joint coordinates over a temporal sequence. Unlike RGB data, which is sensitive to background and environmental noise, skeleton-based methods isolate biomechanical structure at lower computational cost. Serve-subtype classification in this study is a constrained instance of skeleton-based HAR: a fixed-length keypoint sequence is mapped to one of a small set of stroke labels.

**Homography**

Homography is a projective transformation establishing a mapping between two planes, the image plane captured by the camera and the real-world plane of the playing surface (Alemán-Flores et al., 2014). Because the camera observes the court from an elevated, angled viewpoint, image pixel coordinates do not correspond directly to court coordinates. Using a set of known reference points, typically court line intersections, a transformation matrix is computed that maps any pixel lying on the court surface to its corresponding real-world position, without calibration hardware or 3D reconstruction. The matrix form and solution are given in Section 3.3.

**Object Detection** 

Object detection aims to locate, classify, and label existing objects in any one image with rectangular bounding boxes to show the confidences of existence (Zhao et al., 2019). Object detection methods can be categorized into two main types. The first is a traditional object detection pipeline, generating region proposals and then classifying each proposal into different object categories. The second views object detection as a regression or classification problem and adopts a unified framework to achieve final results, the categories and their locations, directly. This includes tracking fast-moving objects such as balls and implements across frames.

**Signal Fusion**

Signal fusion combines information at the input, feature or decision level (Yang & Gulbahar, 2025; Li et al., 2023). Its benefit depends on the signals and evaluation conditions. The comparison implementation uses probability-level GRU–kNN5 fusion; the selected implementation uses GRU alone for subtype prediction and a separate rule layer for combining classification with available measurements. The optional landing stream is inactive in the current evaluation.

**Bounce Detection**

Bounce detection is the process of identifying the moment a ball makes contact with the playing surface by monitoring changes in its vertical trajectory across consecutive frames. During a ball's flight, its vertical position decreases as it falls toward the surface; a bounce is identified when this downward movement reverses to an upward direction, indicating ground contact has occurred (Ning et al., 2023). 

**Categorical Placement Zones**

In sports analytics, raw spatial coordinates are often translated into categorical zones to align with practical coaching terminology and tactical execution (Olthof & Davis, 2025). Categorical placement zones discretize the playing court into distinct tactical areas (e.g., Deep-Left, Short-Right) rather than relying on continuous mathematical measurements. This abstraction allows a rule-based expert system to easily evaluate the tactical intent and legality of a stroke by mapping a continuous 2D coordinate to a finite set of strategic outcomes. In this study, categorical placement zones are assigned exclusively within the optional dual-camera auxiliary module, activated only when a secondary camera is available to supply reliable ball landing coordinates.

## **3.3 Theoretical Foundations** {#3.3-theoretical-foundations}

***Spatial Feature Extraction via Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)***

Computer systems do not naturally understand how a raw matrix of RGB pixels translates into recognizable anatomical structures. Therefore, the use of Machine Learning (ML) models, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), is essential for spatial feature extraction. A CNN applies mathematical filters to input data to detect low-level features (such as edges and gradients) and aggregates them into high-level semantic features (Krichen, 2023). This process is driven by the discrete convolution operation, where learnable filter weights slide across the input image to produce feature maps that isolate specific spatial patterns.

The dimensions of these feature maps are controlled by the network's hyperparameters, such as the filter size, padding, and stride. Adjusting these parameters dictates the resolution and level of detail captured, giving CNN architectures the flexibility to optimize for lower computational requirements (like basic object bounding boxes) or higher computational requirements (like precise anatomical keypoints). Because a single convolution only extracts low-level data, CNNs stack multiple convolutional layers hierarchically. Early layers extract basic textures, while deeper hidden layers aggregate those shapes into complex semantic entities, such as a human joint, a paddle, or a court boundary. While this completes the localized extraction for a single static image, analyzing a physical athletic maneuver requires these spatial features to be tracked sequentially through time.

***Temporal Sequence Modeling*** 

Analyzing a physical athletic action such as a pickleball serve requires modeling how those poses change across time, not just individual poses. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) were designed for this purpose, processing sequential data by maintaining a hidden state that carries information from previous time steps; however, standard RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients, making them unable to retain information across longer sequences (Cho et al., 2014). The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) addresses this limitation through two learned gating mechanisms (reset gate & update gate) that selectively retain or discard information from previous time steps. This allows the network to model long-range temporal dependencies without the computational overhead of more complex architectures (Cho et al., 2014). Lin et al. (2021) validated this approach empirically, demonstrating that a GRU operating on pose keypoint sequences extracted from a monocular camera achieved competitive classification accuracy against LSTM while training significantly faster on a dataset of 70 videos, suggesting GRU is viable for small-dataset, pose-based movement classification. In the selected implementation, the original five-fold GRU ensemble supplies the subtype probability vector. The archived comparison hybrid adds a kNN5 branch from timing features. Hip movement is computed separately and deterministically from pose landmarks.

***Original GRU Selection and the Hybrid Comparison***

The selected original GRU classifier averages the class probabilities of its five retained folds. For each class c, p_GRU(c) is the arithmetic mean of those five predictions. The class with maximum probability is displayed; corrective coaching requires that maximum to be at least 0.60. The comparison hybrid averages this GRU vector with a distance-weighted kNN5 vector computed from 32 timing features. That 50/50 combination is not used for the released GRU candidate. In the matched diagnostic comparison, original GRU scored 51.4% and the hybrid 49.7%; the 1.7-point difference does not establish statistically significant or universal superiority.

The term hybrid classifier refers to the earlier GRU–kNN5 comparison. The selected system remains multimodal because the feedback layer combines GRU classification with distinct hip and paddle measurements. Removing kNN does not remove those measurement streams. Neither hip displacement nor paddle orientation is averaged into GRU subtype probabilities. GRU development accuracy, diagnostic accuracy, coaching coverage and expert-rated feedback validity remain separate measures.

***Late Fusion for Heterogeneous Modalities*** 

The reviewed fusion literature distinguishes early input fusion, intermediate representation fusion and late decision fusion for heterogeneous signals (Yang & Gulbahar, 2025; Li et al., 2023). The present study keeps pose classification, hip measurement and paddle measurement separately inspectable and combines their outputs in deterministic rules. This design avoids requiring a paddle measurement for a subtype prediction, but does not guarantee equal signal quality or increased accuracy. A global GRU confidence gate can still withhold coaching even when a measurement is available.

***Geometric Homography and Planar Coordinate Mapping*** 

To resolve perspective distortions, systems utilize a planar homography (Alemán-Flores et al., 2014). Homography is a perspective transformation that maps points from the image scene plane directly onto an actual reference plane. Mathematically, this is represented in a 3x3 matrix, commonly denoted as H, as illustrated in Figure 2\. If a minimum number of court primitives, such as intersecting white lines, are visible in the scene, they can be matched to the known physical dimensions of the actual court. By mapping these known reference points, the system can solve a linear equation to calculate the exact values of the homography matrix H. Once the matrix is calculated, applying this transformation to any raw 2D pixel coordinate p, denoted mathematically as H(p), instantly projects that pixel into a precise, real-world 2D spatial coordinate on the reference plane.

**Rule-Based Feedback System** 

Expert-grounded rule-based systems represent a well-established approach to automated coaching feedback, operating on the principle that classification outputs trigger pre-validated corrective responses defined by domain specialists rather than generated dynamically. Wang et al. (2019) demonstrated this classify-then-correct structure in practice, using a spatiotemporal pose estimation model with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier to detect bad poses in freestyle skiing and returning exemplar-based visual suggestions to the athlete, establishing that pose classification can serve as the trigger for structured coaching intervention. However, Wang et al.'s feedback was exemplar-based rather than textual, and their rules were derived from the classification output alone without explicit expert validation of the feedback content itself. This distinction matters as a rule-based system is only as reliable as the domain knowledge encoded within it, and without coach validation of the feedback strings, the system risks producing technically correct classifications paired with invalid advice. In this study, researchers use Coach B’s form comments to inform a limited set of deterministic rules. The frozen outputs are then presented to Coach C in Session 2 for contextual validity judgments. This pending review does not constitute prior approval of every feedback string, and it is not blinded to the output being evaluated.

## **3.4 Existing Technologies & Frameworks** {#3.4-existing-technologies-&-frameworks}

**MediaPipe**

MediaPipe, introduced by Lugaresi et al. (2019) as a cross-platform framework for building perception pipelines, provides the deployment infrastructure that enables machine learning models to run on mobile devices through graph-based calculators, streaming support, and GPU acceleration. Its architecture abstracts hardware-specific optimizations, allowing models like BlazePose to perform on-device inference on smartphones without requiring server-side computation. A known limitation of MediaPipe is that its mobile optimization prioritizes inference speed over peak accuracy, a general constraint of mobile-optimized pipelines. 

**BlazePose**

BlazePose, introduced by Bazarevsky et al. (2020) as a two-stage pose estimation model running within the MediaPipe framework, detects 33 body keypoints through a lightweight detector followed by a landmark model optimized for on-device mobile inference. Its 33-keypoint skeleton provides the joint-level resolution across the shoulder, elbow, and wrist sequence necessary for serve swing classification as shown in Figure 1\. A known limitation is reduced tracking accuracy at distal joints, specifically the wrist and elbow, during high-velocity motion, a trade-off inherent to its mobile-optimized architecture (Roggio et al., 2024). BlazePose exposes a pseudo-depth coordinate per landmark; this study discards it and uses only the image-plane coordinates, because the pseudo-depth is not metrically calibrated and the study's claims are restricted to what a monocular view supports. In this study, hip-center landmarks also provide a normalized horizontal movement range. This deterministic proxy is separate from the GRU classifier and does not directly establish foot loading or force transfer. Performance for unrepresented body configurations has not been evaluated.

**TensorFlow Lite**

TensorFlow Lite (TFLite), developed by Google as a lightweight inference framework for mobile and embedded devices, provides the deployment pipeline for running trained deep learning models on ARM-based smartphones without server-side computation (Verma et al., 2021). TFLite converts trained TensorFlow models into a compact flatbuffer format via its MLIR-based converter, which the on-device interpreter then executes using CPU kernels optimized for the ARM Neon instruction set, with optional GPU delegate support for floating-point acceleration on Android and iOS (Verma et al., 2021). A known limitation is that TFLite's GPU delegate does not support quantized models on Android, meaning quantized GRU inference will execute on CPU, introducing higher latency than GPU-accelerated alternatives (Verma et al., 2021). 

**YOLOv26s**

YOLOv26 is a real-time object detection architecture that eliminates both Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) post-processing and the Distribution Focal Loss (DFL) module present in earlier YOLO generations, instead producing direct, non-redundant bounding box predictions through a native end-to-end detection head (Sapkota et al., 2026). Training stability and small-object detection accuracy are further addressed through Small-Target-Aware Label Assignment (STAL) and Progressive Loss Balancing (ProgLoss), which together improve recall on small or occluded instances relative to earlier YOLO generations that lacked targeted mechanisms for this problem (Sapkota et al., 2026). For this study, the small-scale variant is selected: YOLOv26s achieves 48.6% mAP50-95 on the COCO validation benchmark using 9.5 million parameters and 20.7 billion FLOPs, with a CPU ONNX inference latency of 87.2ms (Sapkota et al., 2026). Despite STAL's improvements, small fast-moving objects such as a pickleball remain inherently difficult for lightweight detectors to localize reliably across consecutive frames due to their limited pixel footprint.

**OpenCV minAreaRect**

OpenCV’s minAreaRect is a computational geometry function that calculates the minimum area rotated bounding rectangle enclosing a given 2D object contour (OpenCV, 2025). Unlike standard bounding boxes that remain rigidly aligned to an image's axes, this algorithm rotates alongside the detected object to mathematically extract its precise center, dimensions, and angle. While extracting athlete kinematics is well-established in racket sports (Edriss et al., 2025), applying minAreaRect to the implement itself allows this system to extract the continuous paddle angles required for comprehensive stroke evaluation. However, contour-based angle estimation is highly sensitive to edge distortion. In this study, it is anticipated that motion blur from high-velocity serve swings will degrade the paddle's segmented boundary, potentially causing unstable angle estimations across frames. 

**Homography-based Mapping**

Homography is a projective transformation mapping a camera's 2D image plane to the real-world playing surface (Alemán-Flores et al., 2014). It calculates a transformation matrix using known reference points, like intersecting court lines, to project detected pixels into real-world coordinates without 3D hardware. Because a single camera lacks depth perception, monocular reconstruction is subject to geometric ambiguity where different physical states can produce nearly identical 2D projections, limiting how reliably certain trajectory parameters can be recovered without additional constraints (Grad et al., 2026); homography sidesteps this by bypassing depth entirely and working in the 2D court plane instead. Ball landing points can themselves be detected directly from image-space motion analysis on a monocular camera (Ning et al., 2023), with this study chaining both within the optional dual-camera auxiliary module, accepting the compounded spatial uncertainty that results from combining two processes with fundamentally different error sources..

**Rule-based Feedback System Implementation** 

A rule-based expert system is a decision-support system that encodes domain knowledge as a structured set of IF-THEN production rules, where each rule specifies a condition evaluated against input data and an output action triggered when that condition is met (Örücü & Selek, 2020). In sports coaching applications, these rules are derived from expert knowledge, typically certified coaches or domain specialists, and map detected movement states to corrective feedback strings delivered to the athlete. Örücü & Selek (2020) demonstrate this structure in practice, using joint angle thresholds derived from a certified trainer to construct a rule table that classifies movement correctness and returns simultaneous corrective warnings to the user. Wang et al. (2019) similarly apply the classify-then-correct structure, where a pose classification output serves as the trigger for pre-defined corrective responses. A known limitation of rule-based systems is that their reliability is strictly bounded by the quality of the domain knowledge encoded within them; rules derived without expert validation risk producing technically triggered but contextually invalid feedback, and the systems cannot generalize beyond the movement types and conditions their rule base was designed to cover. 

## **3.5 Problem Context** {#3.5-problem-context}

**Generalization of pose estimation to sport-specific, high-velocity motion.** 

Systems relying on lightweight Human Pose Estimation (HPE) architectures to analyze athletic performance face significant obstacles when tracking dynamic, sport-specific movements. Mobile-deployable models like BlazePose are inherently optimized for and validated against general in-the-wild images and static datasets (Bazarevsky et al., 2020). When deployed in applied sports motion analysis, the accuracy is often constrained by real-world capture conditions; factors such as camera angles, lighting conditions, and occlusion can significantly degrade model performance (Roggio et al., 2024). Furthermore, direct evaluations benchmarking pose estimation models against marker-based systems reveal that spatial discrepancies are highly joint-dependent rather than uniform across the body. While tracking at the ankle approaches the accuracy of gold-standard methods, systematic errors peak significantly at the hip and knee, a degradation researchers specifically attribute to mislabeled ground truth data in the foundational training datasets (Needham et al., 2021). Critically for racket sports, while these validations establish error baselines for the lower body and shoulder during locomotion and jumping, they entirely omit accuracy metrics for distal extremities like the elbow and wrist (Needham et al., 2021). Independent of these empirical discrepancies, qualitative frameworks assessing the applicability of ML models explicitly rate BlazePose as having only a "Medium" capacity for specialized tasks such as injury prevention and posture analysis (Roggio et al., 2024). While recent applications of the MediaPipe framework have successfully extracted stable kinematics during slow, controlled motions like the pickleball dink shot (Edriss et al., 2025), deploying these constrained models to extract fine-grained skeletal sequences during high-velocity, ballistic strokes remains a persistent technical bottleneck. 

**Monocular depth and trajectory ambiguity.** 

Systems relying on a single, monocular camera for spatial analytics face a fundamental geometric constraint when attempting to measure physical distances and object trajectories. Because a single viewpoint lacks depth perception, the framework suffers from monocular ambiguity, rendering the full three-dimensional flight path of a moving object mathematically unrecoverable without specialized, multi-camera calibration hardware. Grad et al. (2026) demonstrated that this absence of depth information severely limits 3D trajectory reconstruction, causing complex spin-decomposition models to fail compared to simpler approximations. To circumvent the inability to track 3D flight, some computer vision approaches bypass depth entirely by employing planar homography, which calculates a transformation matrix to project 2D camera pixels directly onto a flat, 2D real-world reference plane using known intersecting boundary lines. While studies have shown that line-based homography can accurately calibrate court geometry without 3D modeling (Alemán-Flores et al., 2014\) and that four-frame differential slope analysis can detect 2D ball landing points at real-time speeds, though with a documented accuracy tradeoff of 78.5% at real-time speeds relative to 97.0% for slower deep-learning alternatives (Ning et al., 2023), these mechanisms are typically applied in isolation. Translating dynamic pixel coordinates into actionable real-world spatial data requires chaining these two independently solved problems into a single continuous pipeline. Because 2D object detection and homographic calibration possess fundamentally different failure modes and error sources, chaining them inherently compounds spatial uncertainty rather than resolving it. Consequently, extracting reliable, real-world placement metrics from a single, side-view camera remains a persistent architectural obstacle. This study addresses such obstacles by relocating ball placement detection to an optional dual-camera auxiliary module, providing a separate view of the court while retaining detection and planar-calibration uncertainty. The auxiliary stream is not exercised in the current coach evaluation. 

**Heterogeneous multimodal fusion.** 

Systems attempting to integrate multiple, heterogeneous data streams for holistic motion analysis face a severe architectural obstacle when combining signals of vastly different dimensionalities and sampling rates. In multimodal frameworks, input streams often possess fundamentally different dimensional characteristics and semantics (Yang & Gulbahar, 2025). When attempting to merge a high-dimensional, continuous dataset, such as a full skeletal tracking sequence, with extremely low-dimensional data like a near-scalar paddle angle or a categorical placement zone, the network becomes highly susceptible to modality imbalance. If merged too early in the processing pipeline, the sheer volume and variance of the dominant, dense modality can easily overpower and corrupt the weaker, sparser signals before the network can extract their value (Yang & Gulbahar, 2025). While alternative strategies such as hybrid or feature-level fusion can successfully integrate multimodal inputs when the respective data streams share relatively balanced dimensional proportions (Li et al., 2023), these architectures degrade when subjected to the extreme structural asymmetry inherent in combining multi-joint sequences with single scalar values. Consequently, establishing a unified network architecture capable of preserving the analytical integrity of both dense sequential data and sparse, low-dimensional variables simultaneously remains a persistent, unresolved difficulty in applied signal fusion. 

**Compute constraints for real-time, mobile-deployable inference.** 

Systems engineered for real-time, on-device sports analytics face a persistent tension between predictive model accuracy and the strict computational limitations of mobile hardware. In deep learning-based computer vision, achieving robust spatial resolution typically requires complex network architectures that demand substantial processing power and memory bandwidth. When deploying these frameworks to edge devices like smartphones, the system must process sequential video frames rapidly enough to generate immediate feedback, forcing a deliberate reduction in network complexity to prevent hardware bottlenecking and processing overloads. While existing pose estimation frameworks attempt to navigate this compute constraint, they consistently compromise critical analytical parameters. For example, comprehensive architectures such as OpenPose and HRNet carry high computational overheads that render them inherently unsuitable for seamless, real-time mobile deployment (Roggio et al., 2024). Conversely, lightweight architectures like MoveNet prioritize low-latency mobile inference but extract a restricted topological set of only 17 keypoints, compared to denser 33-keypoint models, and are explicitly rated as having only a "Medium" applicability for motion analysis tasks (Roggio et al., 2024). Consequently, balancing the deep biomechanical fidelity required for accurate sports classification against the rigid processing boundaries of everyday mobile devices remains a standing architectural barrier in applied sports analytics.

# **CHAPTER 4** {#chapter-4}

# **DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY** {#design-and-methodology}

This chapter describes the research setting, data preparation, implemented multimodal pipeline and expert-review procedure. It distinguishes the proposed production design from the recorded-clip configuration actually evaluated. Both Coach C sessions and the Xiaomi recorded-file benchmark are complete as of 12 October 2026; live timing remains unverified. Changes to the initial proposal are disclosed explicitly. A later mobile development branch, reported in Section 5.8, changes automatic acquisition and permits guarded general-mechanics cues despite uncertain subtype classification. It was developed after the expert review and does not alter the frozen configuration or inherit its ratings.

## **4.1 Research Environment and Respondents** {#4.1-research-environment-and-respondents}

### **4.1.1 Research Environment** {#4.1.1-research-environment}

A. Physical/data-collection environment

	Coach A's recording was conducted at Jump Serve Sports Center in Mandaue, while all remaining recordings were conducted in an indoor physical education facility at the University of San Carlos, selected for proximity, controlled environmental conditions, and the absence of venue rental cost. Recordings were conducted under consistent artificial court lighting at different times to simulate common recreational play conditions. The exact time window may vary based on court availability, provided the lighting environment remains stable. This introduces known vulnerabilities to motion blur and reduced contrast during ball detection, and it also means the dataset does not represent daylight play; both are acknowledged in Section 1.4.

The recording protocol specified side-view capture at a nominal 1080p resolution and 60 frames per second, with the serving body and paddle visible. Camera height, shutter settings and secondary-camera placement are capture specifications rather than independently verified performance measurements. The selected evaluation videos have recorded metadata and decoding checks. The evaluation uses prepared clips and does not establish autonomous live triggering or automatic end-of-serve detection.

**Figure 3**

*Camera Setup Diagram*

![][image3]

*Note.* The dotted green lines represent each camera's field of view. 

Figure 3 retains the intended primary side-view and secondary receiving-court arrangement. The primary view supplies pose and paddle information. A second view is required for the proposed auxiliary landing analysis, but paired second-camera recordings were not supplied for the 30-clip Coach C batch. Landing was therefore disabled throughout that evaluation; the diagram does not establish that a synchronized two-camera mobile system was validated.

B. Computational/digital environment

* Training environment

The project used Python, TensorFlow/Keras and associated computer-vision tools for development and model export. The manuscript identifies the ASUS Ascent GX10 at the University of San Carlos as an available training resource. The frozen evaluation preserves its own package inventory and model hashes; access to a workstation does not establish that every experiment ran on the same hardware. TFLite model assets support the Android proof of concept and the recorded-clip desktop runner.

* Inference environment

The planned physical-device validation profiles are a Snapdragon 685 device with 6 GB RAM and Android 14, and a MediaTek Dimensity 7300 Pro 5G device with 8 GB RAM and Android 16. Recorded-file timing is complete on the Xiaomi Note 12; live-capture timing and the second planned device profile remain unverified. The Coach C packet was generated through the desktop recorded-clip runner using Android-compatible legacy assets; the selected original-GRU revision recomputes classifications from the preserved pose caches. This does not establish end-to-end parity with the phone's live capture window or attainment of the two-second target.


  ### **4.1.2 Respondents** {#4.1.2-respondents}

  A. Data-source players (serve recording subjects)

* *Coach A*

Coach A is the professional recording participant described in the recruitment records. The annotated training inventory contains 24 Coach A recordings per recorded subtype, totaling 72 clips. Six additional Coach A clips, two per recorded subtype, were selected for the 30-clip evaluation and checked for clip-level overlap with training. They are new recordings from a participant already represented in training. Professional status is not treated as a ground-truth Good Form label; form judgments come from the coach instruments. Coach A did not supply the independent Session 2 feedback ratings.

* *Training Beginner Players (Beginners 1 and 2\)*

Beginners 1 and 2 were purposively selected as training recording participants. Each contributes 23 clips per recorded subtype to the annotated 210-clip inventory, totaling 69 per beginner. Their beginner status does not establish that every recorded execution has bad form. Coach B's form judgments and comments determine the annotated form information. The three training participants provide limited between-player variation, which is examined through participant-held-out development checks as well as clip-stratified cross-validation.

* *Evaluation Beginner Players (Beginners 3 and 4\)*

Beginners 3 and 4 supply the evaluation beginner recordings. Four clips per recorded subtype were randomly selected from each participant with the recorded selection seed, giving 12 clips each. Combined with six additional Coach A clips, the evaluation includes 30 clips and ten per recorded category. These quotas do not impose a predetermined Good/Bad Form ratio. The 24 beginner selections had been inspected in earlier diagnostic work, although they are absent from the classifier training memberships. The resulting evaluation is a retrospective independent coach review, not an untouched sealed test.

  B. Annotator

Coach B serves as the training-set form annotator and source of qualitative deviation commentary. The actual instrument collects Good Form or Bad Form judgments and deviation comments; the researchers report that the independent serve-type question was removed starting with this instrument. Recorded subtype categories and legacy manifests therefore remain distinct from independently assigned coach subtype labels. Coach B's form annotations and comments inform empirical baseline selection and human-authored feedback rules. A single annotator does not provide inter-rater reliability evidence.

  C. Evaluators

Coach C serves as the independent reviewer of the evaluation clips and feedback. Session 1 collects Good Form or Bad Form judgments and deviation comments without showing model feedback; it does not collect independent serve-type labels. Recorded-category context in the annotation workflow must not be represented as independent classification ground truth. The completed submission contains all 30 form judgments. The researchers authorized private inference before submission, departing from the proposal's annotation-then-inference sequence; outputs were kept from Coach C during Session 1. The approved wording revision was also prepared before the responses were read. Session 2 is planned after a one-day interval and presents each clip with its frozen predicted subtype and approved feedback. The coach selects Valid, Not valid, or No coaching feedback to assess, without access to Session 1 responses through the instrument. The actual interval and form version will be recorded. This separation does not guarantee that earlier impressions are forgotten.

  ## **4.2 Research Instrument or Sources of Data** {#4.2-research-instrument-or-sources-of-data}


  ### **4.2.1 Research Instruments** {#4.2.1-research-instruments}

Three researcher-made instruments organize the actual workflow: a recording-category and dataset inventory, a form-and-deviation annotation instrument, and a feedback-validity instrument. The inventory supplies the intended subtype categories used by classification experiments. Coach B supplies form judgments and commentary for construction, while Coach C reviews the evaluation clips and later their system feedback. The revised instruments no longer ask either coach for a separate subtype-classification response. This change limits independent validation of the taxonomy and must not be hidden by relabeling recording categories as expert classifications.

  *A. Recording-Category and Dataset Inventory*

The inventory identifies clips, participants, source paths, recorded categories and split membership. Drive, Lob and Topspin remain the computational output classes. These categories describe the organization and intended serving tasks of the recordings; they do not by themselves prove that each execution matches the intended subtype. Classification metrics retain the label source recorded for the relevant experiment.

The initial proposal included independent subtype labeling and a possible taxonomy fallback. That expert-labeling task was removed from the actual form workflow. No completed independent taxonomy-distinguishability result or implemented switch to a volley/drop classifier is claimed. Historical metadata describing labels as Coach B annotations must be interpreted alongside the actual form schema and the researchers' clarification. The study reports this provenance limitation rather than inferring subtype labels from free-text form comments.


  *B. Qualitative Error Commentary Instrument*

Coach B evaluates each construction-set clip as Good Form or Bad Form and supplies deviation comments for bad-form cases. The researchers categorize those comments and encode corresponding rules by hand. The feedback engine is deterministic; a language model does not generate advice during inference. The qualitative categories are a framework for rule design, not evidence that all six categories have implemented and validated automatic detectors. The rule base used in the current evaluation is limited to the measurable triggers described in Section 4.3.2.

  *C. Feedback Validation Instrument* 

The actual feedback-validation instrument uses all 30 selected clips. Session 1 records form judgments and comments. Session 2 shows each clip with “Serve classification: [predicted class] | Feedback: [approved string]”; predictions below the unchanged confidence gate are explicitly marked low confidence. Video and section titles contain only the clip identifier. The required choices are Valid, Not valid, and No coaching feedback to assess. The third choice applies when there is no substantive correction or positive coaching assessment, not merely because one measurement is missing. No response is preselected. Session 1 answers and construction annotations are not displayed in Session 2. This is an independent coach's review of visible system outputs; it does not independently measure classification accuracy or improvement in subsequent playing performance.

  ### **4.2.2 Primary Source of Data** {#4.2.2-primary-source-of-data}

The dataset is self-collected. The supplied manuscript reports 812 recorded clips. The annotated inventory used for the thesis-aligned retraining study contains 210 training clips, while the current coach evaluation contains 30 selected clips. Separately, the legacy classifier assets and bundled kNN bank use a broader 438-sample training population, and 175 Beginner 3/4 recordings have been used diagnostically. These populations overlap in documented ways and must not be added together or described as though all recordings outside the 240-clip annotation allocation were computationally unused. Consent and source-recording records are retained with the original materials.

  ### **4.2.3 Data Schema / Feature Definitions**	 {#4.2.3-data-schema-/-feature-definitions}

The implemented schema separates classification, hip movement, paddle orientation and optional landing results. Logical independence means an unavailable measurement can be reported without deleting other available outputs; it does not imply that all computation executes simultaneously. The evaluated configuration and each clip's outputs are frozen before the coach's feedback ratings are collected.

  *1\. Kinematic Classification Stream*

* Processing Mechanism: The original five-fold GRU ensemble processes joint-angle sequences derived from pose landmarks. Its mean class probabilities determine the selected subtype. Hip-center displacement is computed separately and normalized by body height. The kNN5 fusion branch is retained for comparisons but excluded from the selected Session 2 configuration.
* System Output (Serve Type): The maximum-probability Drive, Lob or Topspin label from the original GRU ensemble, with its probability vector and confidence retained. Confidence is not assumed to be calibrated correctness.
* System Output (Hip Movement): A value and below-reference state based on image-plane movement. The internal legacy “weight shift” label is a proxy and does not measure ground forces, foot loading or verified forward weight transfer.

  *2\. Equipment State Evaluation Stream*

* System Input: Paddle detections from the fine-tuned detector and a contour-derived long-axis orientation from OpenCV within five frames either side of the estimated contact frame.
* Processing Mechanism: A reference-band comparison using the available image-plane angle measurements. The contact frame is estimated from wrist motion; it is not manually verified paddle–ball impact.
* System Output: Within-reference, outside-reference, or unavailable orientation. Open/closed directional advice remains disabled because physical paddle-face direction is not validated. Geometric angle extraction must not be described as a verified three-dimensional face-orientation diagnosis.

  *3\. Spatial Outcome Stream*

* *System Input* (Ball Landing Coordinates)**:** Raw pixel data of the ball's impact point detected across consecutive frames, processed as a 2D tuple (x, y) mapped to the planar court reference space.  
* *Processing Mechanism***:** Geometric projection via homography mapping, followed by a bounding-box evaluation to assign the coordinate to a discrete court section.  
* *System Output (Spatial Placement)***:** A discrete, categorical placement zone representing where the ball landed. The system classifies the landing coordinate into one of seven formal zones:  
  * *Valid Serves*: Deep-Left (back half of the service box near the centerline), Deep-Right (back half near the sideline), Short-Left (front half near the NVZ line), and Short-Right (front half near the sideline).  
    * The proposed zones also include Fault-Long, Fault-Wide and Fault-Short. No landing-zone result is part of the present 30-clip evaluation, and the system is not evaluated here as a serve-legality adjudicator.


  ### **4.2.4 Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria** {#4.2.4-inclusion/exclusion-criteria}

The recording protocol specified framing and technical-quality criteria. The completed evaluation checks establish file identity, metadata and sequential decodability. They do not establish that every clip passed a full human audit of contact visibility, motion blur or every original exclusion criterion. Missing measurements are retained and reported rather than removing difficult clips after seeing model outputs.

    

    **Inclusion Criteria**

The intended recording criteria are a visible complete serving motion and sufficient visibility of the relevant landmarks and paddle. Court calibration visibility additionally applies when landing analysis is attempted. For the v2 retraining study, the declared tracking gate requires at least 32 usable source frames, adequate visibility and at least 80% valid coverage. The legacy evaluation retains its own preprocessing and acceptance rules; the stricter development adapter is not substituted into the frozen run.

    **Exclusion Criteria**

Technical failures, insufficient framing or invalid tracking can make a measurement unavailable. The v2 training inventory records one quality rejection from 210 clips. The current Coach C set retains all 30 selected clips, including four with unavailable paddle measurements and eight below the selected GRU confidence gate. No post hoc exclusion based on an unfavorable prediction or feedback message is permitted. The study does not claim that the available checks establish validity for populations or movement conditions absent from its sample.

  ## **4.3 Research Procedure** {#4.3-research-procedure}

The selected Session 2 configuration was amended after Session 1 receipt but before outputs were sent to Coach C. Researchers had already inspected Session 1 judgments. Original GRU was selected using the existing matched diagnostic comparison, not by fitting model weights, thresholds or cue text to those judgments. All 30 clips remain; classifications were recomputed from preserved poses and hip/paddle/contact measurements were reused unchanged. The earlier hybrid outputs remain archived. This chronology is disclosed rather than described as a model frozen before Session 1. Android and desktop now default to original GRU, with phone capture and latency still requiring validation.

The workflow comprises recording and inventory management, expert form annotation, training-only feature/rule development, frozen recorded-clip inference, and independent feedback review. Original clip identities determine splits before augmentation. The evaluation records hashes and checks overlap with training, while explicitly retaining the prior diagnostic exposure of the beginner clips. Private inference during Session 1 is documented as a timing amendment. After the reviewed model and wording are frozen, Session 1 comments are not used to tune that same evaluation version.
